title: How to measure risk: write out worst cases and plan around each before taking a leap
summary: A 2017 essay where Sam Parr lays out his process for deciding on a risky move like quitting a job for a startup. List the worst-case scenarios, build a contingency plan for each, and only then weigh the upside. Writing it down shows that downsides are usually smaller than they feel.

principles.text: Most people are bad at analyzing risk; use a deliberate process instead of gut emotion.
principles.quote: I think most people are HORRIBLE at measuring risk…

principles.text: Start by writing out the exact risk you're deciding on, then list the possible worst-case scenarios.
principles.quote: Write out the risk you’re deciding on.

principles.text: For each worst case, decide if you could be happy if it happened. If not, build solutions that make it nearly impossible.
principles.quote: Address each possible worst case scenario and decide if you’re willing and able to be happy if that scenario happens.

principles.text: Make downside plans concrete with numbers: savings, monthly burn cap, runway, and a fallback job you'd accept.
principles.quote: I have $30k in savings. So as long as I spend less than $3k a month, I’ll have 10 months of runway.

principles.text: Only after you're comfortable with the downsides and confident in your contingency plans should you consider the upside; if you like it, do it.
principles.quote: If I’m comfortable with all the downsides I’ve listed out and am confident that I can execute on the contingency plans all while living a life that I’m willing to live, then I consider the upsides.

principles.text: The value is in the process: writing outcomes down shows downsides are usually not that bad, so emotions stop holding you back.
principles.quote: Most people let their emotions hold them back from doing what they really want.
